entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Last Supper, painted by Leonardo da Vinci between 1495 and 1498, is a seminal work of the Italian High Renaissance, located in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Italy. This mural captures the critical moment from the Gospel of John when Jesus reveals that one of his apostles will betray him, an event that has resonated through centuries of Christian thought and art. The composition, characterized by its innovative use of perspective, emotional depth, and intricate detail, marks a pivotal point in the evolution of Western art and religious representation.

The painting depicts the twelve apostles in dynamic responses to Jesus' announcement, showcasing da Vinci's mastery in portraying human emotion and interaction. The work was commissioned by Duke Ludovico Sforza of Milan as part of a renovation of the convent, symbolizing both the patronage of the arts during the Renaissance and the intertwining of religion and politics. As the painting began to deteriorate due to experimental techniques and environmental factors, it sparked discussions on preservation and restoration that continue to this day.

The Last Supper has not only influenced countless artists but also served as a cultural touchstone in discussions of betrayal, sacrifice, and redemption within Christianity. Its imagery has been reproduced and referenced in various forms of media, from literature to film, ensuring its relevance in contemporary discourse. The painting's ongoing legacy is evident in its continued study in art history programs and its impact on modern artistic movements, demonstrating how a single work can transcend its time and medium.
